source_text: Ὅταν οὖν τὸ μὲν εἷναι ἓν τὸ θεῖον ὡς ἐπὶ τὸ πλεῖστον κἂν μὴ θέλωσι τοῖς πᾶσι συμφωνῆται ἐπὶ τὰς ἀρχὰς τῶν ὅλων παραγινομένοις, ἡμεῖς δὲ κρατύνωμεν τὸν διακοσμήσαντα τὸ πᾶν τοῦτο τοῦτον εἶναι τὸν θεόν, τίς ἡ αἰτία τοῖς μὲν ἐπ᾿ ἀδείας ἐξεῖναι καὶ λέγειν καὶ γράφειν περὶ τοῦ θείου ἃ θέλουσιν, ἐφ᾿ ἡμῖν δὲ κεῖσθαι νόμον, οἵ ἔχομεν ὅ τι καὶ νοοῦμεν καὶ ὀρθῶς πεπιστεύκαμεν, ἕνα θεὸν εἶναι, ἀληθείας σημείοις καὶ λόγοις παραστῆσαι; Ποιηταὶ μὲν γὰρ καὶ φιλόσοφοι, ὡς καὶ τοῖς ἄλλοις, ἐπέβαλον στοχαστικῶς, κινηθέντες μὲν κατὰ συμπάθειαν τῆς παρὰ τοῦ θεοῦ πνοῆς ὑπὸ τῆς αὐτὸς αὐτοῦ ψυχῆς ἕκαστος ζητῆσαι, εἰ δυνατὸς εὑρεῖν καὶ νοῆσαι τὴν ἀλήθειαν· τοσοῦτον δὲ δυνηθέντες ὅσον περινοῆσαι οὐχ εὕρηνται, ὡς οὐ παρὰ θεοῦ περὶ θεοῦ ἀξιώσαντες μαθεῖν ἀλλὰ παρ᾿ αὐτοῦ ἕκαστος· διὸ καὶ ἄλλος ἄλλως ἐδογμάτισεν αὐτῶν καὶ περὶ θεοῦ καὶ περὶ ὕλης καὶ περὶ εἰδῶν καὶ περὶ κόσμου. Ἡμεῖς δὲ ὧν νοοῦμεν καὶ πεπιστεύκαμεν ἔχομεν προφήτας μάρτυρας, οἵ πνεύματι ἐνθέῳ ἐκπεφωνήκασι καὶ περὶ τοῦ θεοῦ καὶ περὶ τῶν τοῦ θεοῦ. Εἴποιτε δ᾿ ἂν καὶ ὑμεῖς, συνέσει καὶ τῇ περὶ τὸ ὄντως θεῖον εὐσεβείᾳ τοὺς ἄλλους προὔχοντες, ὡς ἔστιν ἄλογον παραλιπόντας πιστεύειν τῷ παρὰ τοῦ θεοῦ πνεύματι, ὡς ὄργανα κεκινηκότι τὰ τῶν προφητῶν στόματα, προσέχειν δόξαις ἀνθρωπίναις.
pass_a_gloss: When therefore the being one divine thing is agreed upon by almost all even if they do not want to, coming to the beginnings of the whole, we however hold that the one who decorated all this is God, what is the reason that for the others it is permitted to say and write about divine things as they wish, but for us a law is laid down, we who have and think and have rightly believed that one God exists, to present with signs of truth and words? For poets and philosophers, as with the others, have thoughtfully approached, having been moved by sympathy with the breath from God under the soul which each has, to seek and understand the truth if possible; but having been able as much as to think around they have not found, as not having asked to learn about God from God but from each themselves; therefore each of them has dogmatized differently about God and about matter and about forms and about the world. We however have prophets as witnesses of what we think and have believed, who with inspired spirit have spoken out about God and about the things of God. You would say also, surpassing the others in understanding and in reverence for what is truly divine, that it is irrational having abandoned faith in the spirit from God, as if the mouths of the prophets were instruments set in motion, to pay attention to human opinions.

choices.english: as if instruments set in motion

pass_b_english: Even if they refuse to admit it, almost everyone agrees that the divine is one when they reach the first principles of all things. We, however, maintain that the One who ordered this whole universe is God. So why are others free to say and write whatever they wish about the divine, while we who possess the truth, who think and have rightly believed that one God exists, are bound by a law forbidding us to demonstrate this with signs of truth and reasoned arguments? For poets and philosophers, like everyone else, approached the question thoughtfully. Moved by a sympathy with the breath from God within each soul, they sought to find and understand the truth, if possible. Yet they only managed to speculate; they never found it. They did not ask to learn about God from God, but from themselves. Consequently, each one dogmatized differently about God, matter, forms, and the world. We, on the other hand, have prophets as witnesses to what we think and believe. Inspired by the Spirit, they have spoken out about God and the things of God. You yourselves would say it is irrational to abandon faith in the Spirit from God — who moved the mouths of the prophets like instruments — and instead pay attention to human opinions, since you surpass others in understanding and in reverence for what is truly divine.

review.notes: The translation accurately captures the nuances of the Greek text. Pass A provides a literal rendering, and Pass B provides a fluent English version that maintains the theological distinctions and causal relations (e.g., the relationship between the divine breath and the soul, and the distinction between learning 'about' God vs 'from' God).
